extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics; readers interested in Greek numerical notation and ancient arithmetic methods
extracted.subtask_description: A historical/textbook exposition of how the Greeks (and Egyptians/Pythagoreans) performed and conceptualized arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, extraction of roots) and of Pythagorean ideas about number. The page describes concrete algorithms, representational conventions, and conceptual definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate powers of ten for addition and subtraction
rubrics_metrics.description: In writing down numbers for the purpose of these operations, the Greeks would keep the several powers of 10 separate in a manner practically corresponding to our system of numerals, the hundreds, thousands, &c., being written in separate vertical rows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical examples of sums and subtractions are given; the mental part of the work would be the same for the Greek as for us. Examples from Eutocius illustrate carrying/borrowing and alignment by denominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egyptian multiplication by successive doubling
rubrics_metrics.description: To multiply by any number the Egyptians began by successive doubling, thus obtaining twice, four times, eight times, sixteen times the multiplicand, and so on; they then added such sums of this series of multiples (including once the multiplicand) as were required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to multiply by 13, add once, 4× and 8× the multiplicand; to find 25× add once, 8× and 16×. Division was performed by tentative back-multiplication starting with the same doubling process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek multiplication depends on a multiplication table
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek method, which was different from the Egyptian, depended on the direct use of a multiplication table. A fragment of such a table is preserved on a wax tablet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having a multiplication table was a primary requirement for carrying out direct multiplication rather than using successive doubling. The existence of tables underlies later Greek procedures and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Halving-and-doubling column algorithm (Egyptian/Russian variant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write two columns: (1) multiplier and multiplicand, (2) half the multiplier (rounded down if odd) and twice the multiplicand; continue halving first column and doubling second until 1 appears in first column; strike out rows where the first column is even, then add remaining second-column entries to obtain product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked example: multiplying 157 by 88 yields rows (88,157),(41,314),(20,628),(10,1256),(5,2512),(2,5024),(1,10048); strike rows with even first-column entries and sum remaining second-column numbers to get the product. The explanation links this to omitting equivalents when halving even numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start long multiplications from highest-denomination terms (Greek left-to-right habit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greeks began their multiplications by taking the product of the highest constituents first, i.e. they proceeded as we should if we were to begin our long multiplications from the left instead of the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach raises the need to settle the denomination (power of ten) of products of high powers of ten; Archimedes and Apollonius treat exceptional cases. Ordinary examples (from Eutocius) show the mechanics are essentially the same as modern long multiplication, but performed left-to-right through descending powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apollonius's continued-multiplication method: separate bases and powers of ten
rubrics_metrics.description: Apollonius's system finds the continued product of many factors by (1) separately multiplying the bases (the unit-digits, 'TrvOfJXeves') of the factors and (2) separately multiplying the powers of ten (the ciphers) contained in the factors; the final product is expressed in myriads (10000) and their higher powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method applies only when each factor is (a) a number of units 1..9, (b) an even multiple of ten <100, or (c) an even multiple of 100 <1000. Compute indices of the powers of ten (ten=10^1 counts as 1, 100=10^2 as 2), add indices, divide the sum by 4 to obtain the power of the myriad (10000); the remainder (1,2,3) corresponds to extra ciphers (10,100,1000). Example: multiplication of the 38 letters of a hexameter is worked out with indices arithmetic and separate multiplication of bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for ordinary long multiplication (term-by-term descending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the multiplicand first and beneath it the multiplier preceded by eTTL ('by' or 'into'). Take the term containing the highest power of 10 in the multiplier and multiply it into all the terms in the multiplicand in descending order; repeat with the next-highest term of the multiplier, etc.; same procedure applies when numbers contain fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eutocius's examples make the operation clear and show the Greeks maintained the several powers of 10 separately during the work. The final result is obtained by summing the partial products appropriately aligned by denomination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division performed as inverse of multiplication and subtraction, keeping powers separate
rubrics_metrics.description: Division depends on multiplication and subtraction, and was performed 'mutatis mutandis' in the same way as we perform it today: the terms involving successive powers of 10 are mentally kept separate, and successive quotient terms are found by seeing how many times a (power-of-ten) term of the divisor goes into the corresponding term of the dividend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: dividing 1825201 by 1351 proceeds by finding how many thousands go into millions, multiplying divisor by that figure, subtracting, and repeating; Theon's sexagesimal algorithm makes three subtractions per quotient term and is longer and less convenient because it makes it harder to foresee proper trial figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square-root extraction via Euclidean identity and trial division
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract the square root by separating the number into powers of 10, choose the first (highest-denomination) term a (as for quotient in long division), and then use the identity (a + x)^2 = a^2 + 2ax + x^2. Find x by dividing A − a^2 by 2a (and testing) so that 2ax + x^2 is less than the remainder; subtract 2ax + x^2 and continue for further digits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was the actual Greek procedure (illustrated by Theon). For sexagesimal fractions one may scale (multiply by 60^n) to reduce fractional difficulties; Ptolemy/Theon examples show practical considerations and approximations. Trial-and-error is used to choose the maximal admissible x at each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cube-root extraction relies on cubic binomial expansion (but little extant practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of extracting the cube root would depend on (a + x)^3 = a^3 + 3a^2 x + 3ax^2 + x^3, analogous to the square-root method, but no clear extant Greek description survives; Heron gives concrete working without theoretical explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greeks may have relied on tables of cubes for most needs; Heron's approximate procedure shows they had some method, but the theoretical derivation is not extant in surviving writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of multiplication tables for direct Greek multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: One necessary ingredient for the Greek direct-multiplication method was a multiplication table; the Egyptians seem not to have had such a table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A preserved fragment of a Greek multiplication table (wax tablet) supports this; the availability of tables distinguishes the Greek approach from Egyptian doubling-based methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability constraints of Apollonius's method (limits on factor sizes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apollonius's method is confined to multiplying factors each of which is either (a) a number of units 1..9, (b) a number of even tens 10,20,...,90, or (c) a number of even hundreds 100,200,...,900; it does not deal with factors above hundreds (e.g. 1000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation arises because the Greek numeral alphabet only went up to 900 and then restarted for 1000,2000,...; the technique of separating bases and ciphers is designed for this domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of unit and number in the Pythagorean/ancient sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The One (unit) was reasonably regarded as not being itself a number but as the beginning or principle of number; a unit was defined by Thymaridas as 'limiting quantity' or 'limit of fewness'. Number was defined (by Thales and others) as a collection of units, by Eudoxus as a 'determinate multitude', and by Nicomachus as 'a flow of quantity made up of units'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These conceptual definitions underpin the ancient treatment of arithmetic and number theory: unit as principle, numbers as multitudinous compositions of units, and debates about whether the unit counts as a number are noted (Aristotle, Nicomachus, Iamblichus references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ancient classification of numbers: definitions of odd and even
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient/Pythagorean definitions: an even number is that which admits of being divided into two equal parts (the dyad as the principle of the even); an odd number is that which cannot be so divided but is only divisible into two unequal parts. Nicomachus gives alternative formulations: an even number can be divided into both equal and unequal parts (except the fundamental dyad), while an odd number, however divided, must fall into two unequal parts of different kinds (one odd, one even).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions reflect early conceptualizations (and changes) such as the special status of 2 (the dyad) and the way Pythagoreans saw numbers as having qualitative kinds (odd, even, even-odd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pythagorean doctrine: numbers as principles and as having magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Pythagoreans are reported to have regarded numbers not only as characteristics of things but as the principles or elements of all things: 'all things which can be known have number' and 'all things are numbers'; they also supposed the units to have magnitude and constructed the heaven out of numbers (with musical harmonies illustrating numerical ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's discussion highlights both the doctrine (numbers as causes/principles, numbers with magnitude) and its problems (how the 'number in the heaven' relates to abstract numerical attributions). The Pythagorean practice of representing numbers with pebbles and geometric arrangements is cited as illustrative.
